segments: ... and after him to his sons.
Others, however, justify the elder Abu Bakr, his father-in-law, in the first place,
and 'Ali in the fourth.
And some of them, in the matter of belief,
are like those who say that God is a body —
glory be to His grace! —
and that He physically reclines upon a physical chariot that is much larger than heaven and earth.
Others, however, confess Him to be incorporeal,
yet visible to eyes of flesh:
the righteous shall see Him at the resurrection.
And like some
who say that He speaks by an eternal Word subsisting in Himself,
and lives by eternal Life.
Others, while shrinking from the hypostatic doctrine of the Christians,
and yet unable to acknowledge His Word and His Life (His Spirit) to be accidental and temporal,
are forced to say that He indeed speaks,
yet not by a word,
and also lives,
yet not by life.
And like some who say
that God created the sinner in order that he should sin and burn in Gehenna,
and created the righteous in order that he should shine and delight in Paradise;
and He is not to be asked, 'Why?' and man has no free will.
Others, however, confirm free will like the Christians.
And lest we wander beyond the mark,
let us return to our narrative.
And because the kingdom of the Arabs stripped that of the Romans from our regions,
we shall set forth concerning it the events just as they happened,
as we have been informed of them either from reading or from hearsay.
After Muhammad, Abu Bakr {OCR?}: two years.
He sent four commanders of the army to Palestine, to Egypt, to Persia, and to Arabia, against the Christian Arabs.
And he who came to Palestine went against Caesarea.
Now Sergius the patrician gathered a force of Romans and of Samaritans {OCR: Namraye?}, about five thousand foot-soldiers.
And when they met the Romans,
the Arabs gained the upper hand and first destroyed the Samaritans.
When the patrician saw that the people who were with him were defeated,
he turned his back.
And the Arabs pursued after the Romans,
and cut them down like reapers cut ears of corn.
Now it happened that Sergius fell from his horse,
and his servants gathered and mounted him.
And again he fell,
and again they mounted him, and again he fell, three times.
And when they wished to mount him again, he said to them:
"Save your lives,
and leave me to die alone,
and not..."
